newsitem.title: PERU: Bolivia ransom funded Peru attack - police sources.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia ransom funded Peru attack - police sources.

text.p: Ransom money from a kidnapping in Bolivia financed the daring strike by Marxist rebels holding more than 140 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, anti-terrorist police sources said on Monday.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) obtained $1.2 million when it released Bolivian business magnate, Samuel Doria Medina, held captive for 46 days late last year, the sources said.

In an operation directed by the leader of this week's hostage-taking, Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the ransom money was then spirited through Uruguay and Panama before about $800,000 reached the group in Peru, they added.
In an intelligence swoop later on the MRTA rebels involved in the kidnapping, police allowed Cerpa to go free after he produced a Bolivian passport, one source said.

The MRTA, which started as a Robin Hood-style band robbing the rich to give to the poor, was "scrupulous" in using the Doria ransom money to train its members and buy arms for last Tuesday's assault, a source said.
Throughout its 14-year history, the group has kept strong links with revolutionaries in neighbouring Bolivia, whose prisons hold several MRTA guerrillas.
The MRTA had "a relationship with the National Liberation Army, constantly using Bolivia as a safe haven," one source said.
It was not certain whether the rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's residency had included MRTA guerrillas imprisoned in Bolivia in their demand for the release of jailed comrades.

But Mauricio Balcazar, Bolivia's communications minister, has reported receiving a "verbal report" that the MRTA demanded the release of four rebels from his country's jails in exchange for Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, held at the residence.
